**Choice: candidate 4** (moderate confidence). I estimated this in my head from the forecast averages; no simulation was run.

I first checked total volume, then how well each delivery covers the days until the next one arrives.

**Total demand.** Product 0 deliveries can only cover days 4–29. Forecast demand for those days is about 749, or about 783 after the ×1.046 bias. Product 1 deliveries cover days 5–29.

**Candidates 2, 6 and 7 order too much.**
- Candidate 2 orders 937 units of product 0, about 1.25× forecast demand.
- Candidate 6 orders 919, about 1.3× forecast demand.
- The extra 130–150 units are lost: some overflow the 152-unit warehouse, and the rest are left over after day 29. That costs about 1,500.
- Candidate 7 delivers every 4 days in large batches (up to 130 of product 0 plus product 1 stock). That fills the warehouse and causes overflow when demand varies.

**Candidate 3 orders too little.** It orders 737 units of product 0, short of the ~783 expected. A missed unit of product 0 costs 12 (lost margin 6 plus penalty 6), so this loses about 550, plus more when demand runs high.

**Candidates 0, 1 and 4 order about the right amount** (~820 units of product 0, a buffer of ~40).
- Candidates 0 and 1 order every 3 days, so they pay 9 × 47 in fixed order fees. Each has a product 1 batch that is too small for the days it has to cover:
  - candidate 0: 18 units for about 41 units of demand on days 10–12;
  - candidate 1: 22 units for about 34 on days 11–13.

  Missed product 1 sales cost about 9 per unit, so each loses roughly 100–150. Each also runs short on product 0 around the day-10 spike (55): candidate 0 on days 9–11, candidate 1 on days 7–12.
- Candidate 4 orders every 2 days, which costs about 188 more in order fees. Each delivery is about 1.1× the forecast for the days it covers, with no gaps, for both products. Smaller deliveries also mean less stock on hand: about 175 less in storage costs and less risk of overflowing the warehouse.

**Candidate 5** orders the same product 0 as candidate 4, but bundles product 1 into 4-day batches. Its order fees are the same, but storage costs and overflow risk are higher, so it is worse than candidate 4.

Overall, candidate 4's extra order fees are roughly cancelled by its lower storage costs. Its lack of shortage gaps is what puts it ahead of candidates 0 and 1.

I pick **Candidate 4**, but not with high confidence. Candidates 0 and 1 come close because they order less often. I worked this out by hand on the forecast values, as the task required, so the figures below are approximate.

**Total demand.** For days 4–29, when orders can arrive, forecast demand for item 0 is about 749. Multiplied by the average factor of 1.046, that is about 783. For days 5–29, forecast demand for item 1 is about 324, or about 339 after the multiplier. Days 0–3 will run short whatever the plan, so they don't separate the candidates.

**Candidate 4** orders every 2 days: 824 units of item 0 and 356 of item 1, across 13 order days.
- Deliveries track 2-day demand with a margin of about 10%. Item 0 stock builds a buffer of 30–90 units by the second half of the month.
- At forecast demand, stock gets thin only early on (about 5 units on day 5 and 9 on day 7).
- Deliveries are small, so the 152-unit warehouse limit never causes losses.
- At forecast demand about 75 units of item 0 are left at the end, or roughly 40 at actual average demand. That is a moderate waste.

**Candidates 0, 1, 3 and 6** order every 3 days, which saves about 188 in order fees (9 order days instead of 13).
- Candidate 1: even at forecast demand, about 35 units of item 0 are lost on days 22 and 25 because the warehouse is full. Item 0 stock also gets close to zero at forecast demand (2 units on day 12, 5 on day 27). With random demand, both the losses and the shortages get worse.
- Candidate 0 behaves much like Candidate 1.
- Candidate 3 orders too little (737 against roughly 783 needed), so it runs short.
- Candidate 6 orders more (deliveries up to 167), so it loses even more to the warehouse limit.

**Candidate 7** orders every 4 days. Four days of demand is about 167 units, which is more than the warehouse holds, so it overflows and also runs short.

**Candidate 2** orders every 2 days, like Candidate 4, but about 113 more units of item 0 and 28 more of item 1. That extra costs about 1,400. The shortages it would avoid are worth noticeably less, and most of the extra ends up as leftovers at the end of the month.

**Candidate 5** orders the same item 0 quantities as Candidate 4, but item 1 only every 4 days. Item 1 keeps for just 6 days, so random demand makes it waste more and run short more often than Candidate 4.

Overall, Candidate 4 tracks demand most closely and holds up best when actual demand moves away from the forecast. That should outweigh the extra order fees.

**Ответ: −1 («не знаю»).** Я не могу уверенно назвать одного лучшего кандидата. Полностью по шагам я просчитал только кандидата 2, и то до дня 22. Остальных оценивал по тому, как они должны себя вести, без полного расчёта.

**Общее для всех планов:**
- **Нехватка в первые дни неизбежна.** Первые поставки приходят только на 4-й и 5-й день. Поэтому в дни 0–3 при прогнозном спросе не хватает около 59 ед. товара 0 и около 41 ед. товара 1. Неустойка за это — порядка 600 у всех планов.
- **Деньги урезают заказы в дни 3–8 у всех.** Пример для кандидата 2: в день 4 оплачено только 33 ед. товара 0 и ноль товара 1, в день 6 — 76 ед. товара 0 и 1 ед. товара 1. В итоге в дни 10–12 у него есть нехватка. Подробно урезания я проверил только у кандидата 2. У остальных оценил грубо: кандидат 1 упирается в деньги уже в день 3, и при прогнозном спросе урезания должны примерно сглаживать разницу между планами в первой половине срока.

**Что видно по отдельным кандидатам:**
- **Кандидаты 6 и 7, скорее всего, хуже.** У кандидата 7 партия 118 + 60 = 178 больше вместимости склада (152), часть точно пропадёт. У кандидата 6 большой запас тоже грозит переполнением.
- **Кандидат 3, вероятно, хуже других.** Он заказывает ровно по прогнозу, а средний множитель спроса около 1,046. Значит, нехватка будет систематической, и каждая недостающая единица товара 0 обходится примерно в 12.
- **Кандидат 5, видимо, немного хуже кандидата 4.** Заказы в те же дни, поэтому и плата за дни заказов та же. Но товар 1 приходит более крупными партиями, а значит, больше хранения и риска списания.
- **Кандидат 2:** в моём расчёте излишек от запаса в 25 % копится на складе. В день 22 склад переполняется: пропадает 24 ед. товара 0, это 264 уже оплаченных денег.

**Почему не выбираю из 0, 1, 2 и 4.** Разница между ними — это несколько противоречащих друг другу эффектов. Заказ раз в два дня стоит примерно на 190 дороже (13 платежей по 47 против 9). Больший запас сокращает нехватку, но повышает риск переполнения и хранение. Кроме того, урезание деньгами в начале съедает часть разницы. Каждый из этих эффектов — порядка сотен, и при разбросе спроса около 30 % в день надёжно отличить лучший план без полного расчёта нельзя.

I'm choosing **candidate 4**, but only with moderate confidence. Candidates 1 and 0 come out about the same on average. Candidate 4 wins mainly because it is safer under random demand. All of this is mental arithmetic, as the task required.

**How much each plan supplies compared with expected demand**
- **Early shortage is the same for everyone.** The first deliveries arrive on day 4 for product 0 and day 5 for product 1, so every plan runs short on days 1–4.
- **Expected demand from first delivery onward:** product 0, days 4–29, is about 749 × 1.046 ≈ 783 units. Product 1, days 5–29, is about 324 × 1.046 ≈ 339 units.
- **Candidate 4** orders 824 units of product 0 and 356 of product 1, about 5% above expected demand. It orders every 2 days, in lots of roughly 60 + 25. That keeps stock well below the 152-unit limit, and leftover stock stays small.
- **Candidate 5** orders the same product 0 as candidate 4 but bunches product 1 into lots of about 60 every 4 days. It orders on the same days, so it saves nothing on the 47 fee. It only adds storage cost and a higher risk of spoilage and overflow, so it is worse than 4.
- **Candidate 2** orders about 937 units of product 0, roughly 150 more than expected demand. At 11 per unit plus storage, that loses about 1,600 or more.
- **Candidate 3** orders only about 737 units of product 0, below expected demand. It loses sales and pays the shortage penalty.
- **Candidates 6 and 7** order too much and in large lots (100–130 of product 0 plus 50–66 of product 1). Each delivery pushes stock past the 152-unit limit, and the excess is lost.
- **Candidates 1 and 0** order about the same totals as 4 (about 820 of product 0, 350 of product 1), but every 3 days. They pay the 47 fee on 9 days instead of 13, saving about 190. Their larger lots cost roughly that much extra in storage. Peak stock reaches about 140–145 units, close to the limit. If demand comes in low, deliveries overflow and the excess is lost.

So on average candidate 4 roughly ties with 1 and 0. It wins because it is safer under randomness: smaller lots, a safe margin below the stock limit, and a supply level matched to demand.

**Choice: candidate 2.** I worked this out by hand, at forecast (mean) demand, so the numbers are approximate. The margin over candidates 4 and 5 is small.

**What decides the outcome: cash in the first week.** The starting stock (32 and 26 units) covers only about one day of demand. The first deliveries arrive on day 4 (good 0) and day 5 (good 1). So days 1–3 bring shortages that no plan can avoid. By days 3–6 the cash runs low and the orders get cut, and those cuts cause new shortages around the spike on days 10–13. Good 0 also loses more per unit short than it costs to hold a unit: a shortage costs about 12 (6 lost margin plus 6 penalty), while a leftover costs 0.4 a day. That favours a larger buffer on good 0.

**Candidates, step by step:**
- **1 (3-day cycle, about 15% buffer):** the day-6 order is cut to 56 units of good 0 and none of good 1. About 42 units of good 0 and 26 of good 1 go short on days 11–13, a loss of about 740. It saves about 190 by paying the 47 fee 4 fewer times.
- **3 (lean 3-day cycle):** day 6 is cut to 75 units of good 0. Early losses are about the same as candidate 1. With no buffer, it runs short more often later when demand comes in high.
- **0:** the day-5 order is cut to 37 units, which leaves about 55 units of good 0 short around day 10. Worse than candidate 1.
- **6 and 7:** big early orders use up the cash, and then the next orders are cut. Candidate 6 leaves about 69 units of good 1 short. Candidate 7 runs into the same cash and capacity problems.
- **4 (2-day cycle, 10% buffer):** the orders on days 4 and 6 are only partly cut. Good 0 goes almost unshort (about 2 units), and good 1 is short about 44 units. The early loss is about 420, and it pays the fixed fee 4 more times than candidate 1. Overall it is about 130 better than candidate 1. Its thin buffer, though, lets it run short later when demand is high.
- **5:** at forecast demand it is almost the same as candidate 4, with a slightly higher risk of good 1 spoiling in its larger batches.
- **2 (2-day cycle, about 25% buffer on good 0):** early losses are close to candidate 4's (good 0 short about 4, good 1 short about 41). Its larger buffer on good 0 should save roughly 300–400 in shortages over days 10–29 when demand is random. Against that, roughly 20 units are left over at the end, worth about 220.

Candidate 2 comes out ahead because its early cash cuts are mild and its good 0 buffer protects best against random demand.

**Choice: Candidate 1.** It's a judgement call made with modest confidence, not a clear win. I did all the arithmetic in my head on the forecast (mean) values. Candidates 0 and 4 come out close behind.

1. **Total ordered against total need.** Orders placed after day 0 arrive between days 4 and 29. Good 0 forecast demand for those days is about 727 units, or about 760 at the mean multiplier of 1.046. Good 1 needs about 339 for days 5–29.
   - **Lean (candidate 3):** 737 of good 0 and 312 of good 1. It runs short almost every cycle, including the day-10 spike. Each short unit costs 12 on good 0 and 9 on good 1 (lost margin plus penalty).
   - **Heavy (candidates 2 and 6):** 937 and 919 of good 0. That leaves about 150 or more units unsold at the end, at 11 each, and stock also overflows at the 152-unit capacity.
   - **Moderate (candidates 0, 1, 4, 5):** about 820 of good 0 and 340–356 of good 1.

2. **Fixed fees.** The 2-day plans (candidates 4 and 5) order 13 times, versus 9 times for the 3-day plans. That costs an extra 4 × 47 = 188. Following stock day by day, their buffers are about the same as candidate 1's, so smoother deliveries don't make up the 188. Candidate 5 is no better than 4: it pays the same fees and its big good 1 batches spoil more. Candidate 7's 4-day batches overflow capacity and run short around the spike.

3. **Candidate 1 against candidate 0.**
   - **Good 0:** Both cover the day-10 spike with tight stock, about 114 against 112 for candidate 1 and 108 against 110 for candidate 0.
   - **Good 1:** Candidate 0 brings only 18 + 10 units for days 10–12, against demand of 41, so it is short by about 13. Candidate 1 is short by about 4.
   - **Capacity and cash:** Neither plan loses much to overflow at the mean multiplier, and cash covers every order in both.

Candidate 1 holds up as well as either rival when demand varies. Its edge over them is roughly 100–200, which is small against the spread that random demand creates.

I pick **candidate 4**, but with low confidence. On average demand, candidates 0, 1 and 4 come out almost the same, and only the risk of overflowing the warehouse tips it toward 4. I worked this in my head, as the task required, so all numbers are rough estimates.

**Demand.** The true average is about 1.046 × forecast. Over 30 days that is about 879 units of product 0 and about 423 of product 1. Days 0–3 run short for every candidate, since their first deliveries can't arrive in time. The starting stock covers 32 of the ~91 forecast units of product 0, so about 60 units go unsold either way.

**Weeding out the weaker candidates:**
- **Candidate 3** buys too little of product 0 (737 + 32 starting stock, against roughly 816 that can actually be sold). That means about 50 or more units short, at a loss of about 12 each.
- **Candidates 2 and 6** buy too much of product 0 (937 and 919). The extra stock costs storage and gets thrown out at the end. In candidate 6 the big deliveries also overflow the 152-unit warehouse, for example on day 8.
- **Candidate 7** orders every 4 days in batches of 120–130 units, which keeps running into the warehouse limit.
- **Candidate 5** buys exactly the same product 0 as candidate 4. Its product 1 comes in larger batches every 4 days, which adds storage cost and expiry risk and saves no ordering fees, because it still places orders every second day.

**Candidates 0, 1 and 4:**
- All three buy about the right total: about 853 units of product 0 including starting stock, and 341–356 units of product 1.
- On forecast demand each builds a similar buffer of about 71–75 units of product 0 by the end. Each is also thin at the start, around days 9–12.
- Candidates 0 and 1 order every 3 days, so they pay 4 fewer ordering fees (about 188 saved). Their larger batches cost about 170 more in storage, so the two effects nearly cancel out.
- The deciding factor is late in the month. Candidates 0 and 1 each deliver more than 100 units of product 0 at once, on day 24 for candidate 0 and day 25 for candidate 1. Added to stock already on hand, that is close to or over 152. Even on average demand they lose units to overflow, and they lose more on low-demand days. Candidate 4 delivers about 60–70 units every 2 days and stays well under the limit.

**Result:** Candidate 4 is somewhat more robust and should do slightly better on average, but the gap is close to the noise.

I pick **candidate 4**: an order every 2 days with a small buffer. This is a rough mental estimate, not a full simulation.

**The deciding factor: total quantity ordered.** I compared how much of good 0 each plan orders against the expected demand those orders must cover (days 4–29). The forecast for those days sums to 749; times the average multiplier of 1.046, that is about 783. Any unit that never sells is a pure loss of 11. Buying one more unit costs 11 and earns 17 + 6 = 23 if it sells, so the right total is close to the expected demand.
- Candidate 2 orders 937 and candidate 6 orders 919. That is about 140–150 units too many, worth roughly 1,500–1,700 in leftover stock.
- Candidate 3 orders 737, about 46 short of expected demand. Each missing unit costs 12, and random demand makes the shortfall larger still.
- Candidates 4, 1, 0 and 5 order 820–824, which is close to the right level. For good 1 they order 350–356 against an expected 339, which is also reasonable.

**Comparing the plans that order about the right amount:**
- **Candidate 0:** the batch ordered on day 5 is 90 units, but it has to cover days 9–11, including the day-10 spike. Expected demand for those days is about 115, so roughly 25 units go short (about 300 lost).
- **Candidate 1:** the 100 units ordered on day 6 arrive on day 10 and must cover days 10–12, where expected demand is about 117. That means shortages at the spike. Cash on day 6 is also tight: about 1,350 available against 1,279 needed. Ordering every 3 days instead of every 2 saves about 188 in order fees, but holding about 13 extra units of good 0 and 7 of good 1 costs about the same (~170).
- **Candidate 4:** I followed the cash day by day and no order gets cut. On day 6 it has about 1,297 against 1,209 needed. Its batches follow the forecast closely, including the spike: 92 units for days 10–11 against an expected demand of about 88. Arrivals stay well under the 152-unit capacity.
- **Candidate 5:** it pays the same order fees as candidate 4, but its larger good 1 batches mean more holding cost and more risk of good 1 spoiling (6-day shelf life).
- **Candidate 2** has an extra problem: on day 6 it has about 1,002 against 1,364 needed. The order gets cut to 86 units of good 0 and none of good 1, so good 1 runs short on days 11–12.

**Risk:** candidate 4's buffer is thin, so it will run short on high-demand days. Still, its total stays close to expected demand, its cash never cuts an order, and it doesn't hit the capacity limit, so it holds up best when demand deviates from the forecast.

I'm declining to pick (choice = −1). Plans 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 look too close to separate with reasonable confidence.

**What decides the outcome**
- **Early cash is the main constraint.** Some shortage on days 0–4 can't be avoided whatever the plan: deliveries only start on day 4 (good 0) and day 5 (good 1). After that, every plan is short of cash around days 4–6.
- **Candidate 1, traced on forecast demand:** the day-6 order gets cut to about 52 units of good 0 and 1 of good 1. That leaves a shortage on day 11. The day-15 order also loses all of good 1, which causes shortages on days 21–22. Then 12 units of good 0 are lost to the 152 capacity limit on day 25, and about 55 units of good 0 expire unsold at the end. The profit comes out around 2750 on forecast demand. Real demand averages about 4.6% higher, which raises the number somewhat.
- **Candidates 6 and 7** are clearly weaker. Their large batches overflow the capacity limit, the early cash cuts are harsher, and candidate 7 has a long gap before the day-10 spike.
- **Candidate 0** places its order on day 5, when it has even less cash, to cover the spike.
- **Candidates 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5** trade off against each other:
  - Ordering every two days costs about 188 more in order fees.
  - In return, those plans get smaller cash cuts, no capacity losses, and less waste at the end.
  - The lean plan 3 runs out of stock more often, and each unit short on good 0 costs about 12 (6 lost profit plus 6 penalty).

These effects are roughly the same size, with an uncertainty of a few hundred in either direction. That isn't enough to name a best plan.

**Choice: candidate 4.** I simulated each plan day by day on the mean demand (forecast × 1.046) and roughly estimated the expected shortfall per order cycle. All numbers below are rough mental estimates.

**Demand to cover.** Product 0 deliveries arrive from day 4 on, and demand from then is about 783 units. Product 1 deliveries arrive from day 5 on, and demand from then is about 339. Before that, starting stock runs short whatever the plan.

**Plans dropped right away:**
- **Candidates 3 and 7** order too little of product 0 (737 and 760). That means about 25–45 units of lost sales and penalties, at 12 each. Candidate 3 is also short on product 1.
- **Candidates 2 and 6** order too much product 0 (937 and 919). Each has about 100–140 extra units that go unsold, at 11 each. Candidate 6 also runs into the 152-unit warehouse limit.
- **Candidate 5** has the same product 0 orders as candidate 4. It just batches product 1 every 4 days, so it pays the same daily order fees with less precise product 1 stock. It is strictly worse than candidate 4.

**Candidate 4 against candidates 0 and 1 (3-day cycle, 9 orders):**
- **Order fees:** candidate 4 places 13 orders instead of 9, so it pays about 188 more.
- **Holding:** smaller deliveries every 2 days mean less stock on hand, saving about 160.
- **Product 0 shortages:** candidates 0 and 1 have almost no buffer early on. They miss part of the day 10–12 demand spike (forecast 55 on day 10), leaving about 9 units short on average. Expected shortfall is about 27 units for candidate 1 versus about 10 for candidate 4, which saves about 200.
- **Product 1 shortages:** both candidates 0 and 1 order very little for the cycle starting day 10/11. Candidate 1 is about 10 units short on average and candidate 0 about 18. Expected shortfall is about 17 units for candidate 1 versus about 3–4 for candidate 4, which saves about 125. Candidate 0 does even worse here.
- **Leftover at the end:** similar for all, with candidate 4 slightly less.
- **Warehouse limit:** candidate 0 hits it around day 24 and candidate 1 comes close. Candidate 4 stays well under.

**Robustness.** Candidate 4's buffers grow steadily and it reorders more often, so it handles demand swings best.

Overall, candidate 4 comes out ahead of candidate 1 by roughly 300, and candidate 1 beats candidate 0.

I pick **candidate 4**, but with only moderate confidence. Candidates 0, 1, 4 and 5 are probably within a few hundred of each other, and every plan runs into the same cash shortage around day 6.

**Losses every plan shares.** No order arrives before day 4 for good 0 or day 5 for good 1. So the early shortages are the same for all candidates: about 59 units of good 0 and 54 of good 1, roughly 670 in penalties. These penalties leave cash at nearly zero by days 3–5. As a result, the order placed for the day-10 spike gets cut short in almost every plan.

**Plan by plan, on the forecast values:**
- **7** (every 4 days, big batches): cash runs out early and the batches risk overflowing the 152-unit warehouse. Worst.
- **2 and 6** (25–30% buffer): they order about 920–940 units of good 0 against an expected demand of about 783. That leaves 140–160 units to spoil or sit unsold at the end, costing more than 1,500 in purchases. Cash also cuts their early orders harder.
- **3** (no buffer): it orders 737 units of good 0, below expected demand. The day-6 order is cut to 75, and days 11–12 have no arrivals, so it falls short by about 37 units. It is short over the whole horizon as well.
- **0**: the day-5 order is cut from 90 to 37 units of good 0 and to zero of good 1. That leaves about 55 units of good 0 short around the spike, roughly 660 lost, plus about 30 units of good 1.
- **1**: the day-6 order is cut to 56 units of good 0 and zero of good 1. It ends up about 42 units of good 0 and 26 of good 1 short. Its batches of 100–108 also approach the warehouse limit around days 16–22.
- **4** (every 2 days, about 10% buffer): cash still cuts its orders on days 4 and 6. But smaller, more frequent arrivals cover the spike: only about 2 units of good 0 are short, plus about 45 of good 1. It never comes close to the warehouse limit. It pays about 190 more in order fees than the 3-day plans, but saves about the same on holding costs.
- **5**: identical to 4 for good 0. For good 1 it orders in 4-day batches that only keep 6 days, so leftovers spoil more. Slightly worse than or equal to 4.

**Randomness.** These are fixed orders with no adjustment, so surpluses and shortages pile up over time. A moderate buffer with frequent orders (4) handles that better than big infrequent batches (0, 1), which risk overflow, or large buffers (2, 6), which mean spoilage.

I picked **candidate 1** after rough mental arithmetic. I did not simulate any plan in full, so this is a judgement call, not an exact ranking.

**Candidate 1 (3-day cycle, about 15% buffer on good 0)**
- **Coverage.** Each good-0 batch covers its three days of forecast demand with a small surplus: 80 against 70, 80 against 76, 100 against 112 (plus about 14 left over from earlier batches), 86 against 75, 100 against 88, 88 against 77, 108 against 95, 104 against 91, and 74 against 65 for the last two days.
- **Day-10 spike.** It meets the spike without a gap.
- **Cash.** It never runs short: about 360 is left after the day-3 order, and about 1350 is on hand against a day-6 order of about 1280.
- **Capacity.** The 152-unit limit is never exceeded.
- **Fixed fees.** It pays the 47 fee only 9 times.
- **Weak spot.** The day-6 order of good 1 (22 units against about 34 of forecast demand) leaves a small shortage, but good 1 has a low margin.

**Why the others fall short**
- **Candidate 0:** On average it is about as good as candidate 1. But the batch arriving on day 9 is 90 units, plus about 10 left over, against about 110 of demand over days 9–11, so it falls short at the spike. It also pays the fee 10 times.
- **Candidates 2, 4 and 5 (2-day cycle):** They pay the fee 13 times, about 190 more than a 3-day plan, and two days between orders doesn't recover that. Candidates 4 and 5 also carry only a thin buffer, while a missing unit of good 0 costs 12 (6 lost margin plus 6 penalty) and a leftover costs only about 0.4 per day.
- **Candidate 3:** It orders exactly the forecast, but the demand multiplier averages 1.046, so it runs short consistently.
- **Candidate 6:** Cash runs out on days 3 and 6, so those orders get cut just before the spike. Around day 16, stock goes over the 152-unit limit and the excess is lost.
- **Candidate 7:** It has the same cash and capacity problems in a stronger form, and its long 4-day gaps between batches make good-1 spoilage more likely.

**Choice: candidate 2** (a reorder every 2 days with a ~25% buffer on good 0). I worked this out in my head on the forecast values, as the task required. The money figures are rough estimates, not an exact simulation.

**What every plan loses no matter what.** The first deliveries arrive on day 4 (good 0) and day 5 (good 1). The opening stock runs out on day 1, so about 59 units of good 0 and 54 of good 1 go unmet on days 1–4. That costs every candidate the same.

**What separates the plans: cash on days 3–6.** Days 1–3 bring penalties instead of sales, so cash falls fast, and a large early order leaves nothing for the next one. A truncated order shows up 4–5 days later as missing goods around the day-10 spike (55 units of good 0).

- **Candidate 0:** cash on day 3 is about 89. The day-5 order is cut to 36 units of good 0. Over days 10–11 about 56 units of good 0 go unmet, roughly 670 in lost profit plus penalties.
- **Candidate 1:** the day-3 order uses up nearly all the cash. The day-6 order is cut to 53 units of good 0 and 0 of good 1. That means about 45 units of good 0 short on days 11–12 and about 26 units of good 1 short. The total loss is about 770.
- **Candidate 3:** the plan has no buffer, and the day-6 order is also cut, to 73 units. That leaves about 39 units of good 0 short on days 10–12. It also stays short through the whole period, because demand averages ~4.6% above forecast.
- **Candidates 6 and 7:** the orders are even bigger, so cash gets squeezed harder and the 152-unit warehouse may overflow.
- **Candidate 5:** good 1 comes in large batches every 4 days. The day-4 order is cut and good 1 gets nothing. Good 1 then runs out on days 5–12, and some of the big batch spoils.
- **Candidate 4:** the day-4 order is cut to 50 units of good 0 and 0 of good 1. Good 0 still covers the spike. Good 1 ends up about 23 units short, roughly 210 lost.
- **Candidate 2:** the day-4 order is cut too, to 33 units of good 0. But the day-6 order (105 units) goes through in full, and good 0 holds through the spike: 147 units arrive against 146 of demand over days 4–9, then 105 more on day 10. Good 1 is about 18 units short, roughly 160 lost. That is the smallest loss of all the plans.
